questionText:
Read the given passage and answer the four questions that follow
 
Every time a child takes a soft drink, is he laying the ground­work for a
dangerous bone disease? Fizzy and sugary drinks don’t cause
osteoporosis but, because they are often a substitute for a glass of milk,
children miss out on taking in the calcium and vitamin D they need to build
a strong skeleton. Many of them also lead a sedentary lifestyle, so they
aren’t getting the bone­building benefits of vigorous exercise either. These
children tend to suffer from brittle bones and frac­tures later on in life. In
addition, they could be at a risk of being diagnosed with osteoporosis at an
earlier age than most others.
 
Osteoporosis starts in childhood, but its consequences are apparent at a
later stage in life. This condition causes bones to become riddled with
holes, like the framework of a house that has been attacked by termites.
This can lead to broken bones, which in turn, can cause deformity, chronic
pain, and disability. Osteoporosis can be fatal: up to 25 percent of older
people who suffer a broken hip die within a year. Osteoporosis isn’t just
your grandmother’s health threat. Although it strikes over 50 million
women in India, it also menaces over 12 million men.
 
It is important to save millions of people from the risk of suffering from
osteoporosis by adopting preventive measures like walking, jogging or
skipping. Getting enough sunlight, and adequate calcium, especially
through fruits, vegetables and fermented dairy products also helps.

questionText:
One afternoon in late June, as the sun shone warmly into the large
courtyard, a very elegant Victoria, drawn by two sleek black
horses, stopped in front of the mansion. The Countess descended the
steps just as her husband, returning home, appeared at
the carriage entrance.
 

The Count paused, his face turning slightly pale as he observed his wife.
She was strikingly beautiful, with her long oval face, an
ivory-like complexion, large gray eyes, and jet-black hair. Her graceful and
aristocratic demeanour only heightened her appeal.
Without sparing him a glance or acknowledging his presence, she entered
the carriage with a high-bred air that rekindled the
burning jealousy which had long consumed him.
 
Approaching her, he asked in a measured tone, "You are going for a
drive?"
 
She responded coldly, "You see I am."
 
"May I join you?" he ventured, attempting to mask his unease.
 
"The carriage belongs to you," she replied disdainfully, her tone cutting
and dismissive.
 
Without reacting to her hostility, he climbed in and gave the order: "To the
Boulogne Woods" The footman took his place beside
the coachman, and the spirited horses pranced onto the street. Husband
and wife sat stiffly side by side in silence, the tension
between them palpable. He hesitated, seeking a way to begin a
conversation, but her resolute, icy demeanour held him back.
 
Finally, as if by accident, his gloved hand brushed hers. She recoiled
sharply, her gesture laden with unmistakable disgust. He
remained thoughtful, in spite of his usual authoritative and despotic
character, and finally said: "Gabrielle!"

Earlier this year, my daughter moved into college, where I noticed her
neighbour's vision board filled with quotes and photos of
physicians. The neighbour's mother explained it was meant to inspire her
daughter, aspiring to be a pediatrician, to "manifest"
her goal. Manifestation, popularized by The Secret, suggests desires can
become reality through focused thought. Neuro-
scientists James Doty and Sabina Brennan explore how brain function
supports this idea, offering practical approaches to
achieving goals.
 
Doty's Mind Magic dismisses magical thinking, emphasizing a scientific
approach to cultivating resilience and focus. His six-week
plan teaches readers to embed intentions into their subconscious, rewire
brain networks, and improve attention to
opportunities. He argues that manifesting clarifies desires and aligns
thoughts with purposeful action, transforming goals into
reality.
 
Brennan's The Neuroscience of Manifesting also debunks myths around
manifestation, explaining how intentional thinking shifts
perception and behaviour. She highlights the brain's negativity bias and
advocates redirecting attention to positive, goal-
oriented thoughts. Brennan introduces the "seven Cs of manifesting"-
curiosity, compassion, connection, change, clarity,
coherence, and creation - drawing from neuroscience and psychology to
explain how intentional focus can lead to success.

outcomes but rather activating brain networks like the
reticular activation system to reinforce goals. By stimulating focus and
motivation, such tools help translate aspirations into
action. Ultimately, Doty and Brennan remind us that achieving our
ambitions depends on intention, focus, and actionable

As to your studies, I wish you to learn Latin, French, and dancing. I insist
particularly on dancing because it is often neglected yet
crucial to success in life. First impression depends on two things: dress
and address-both within our control. Neglecting these
often leads to slights, coldness, and contempt, which even integrity and
talents cannot always overcome. Ignoring what ensures
others' favourable opinions suggests arrogance or defiance-never without
serious consequences. Neglect of appearance
implies disrespect for others and often stems from poor sense as much as
poor nature. The maxim, "Desire to please, and you
will infallibly please," explains this well.
 
Slovenliness can be cured with effort, but a graceful carriage requires early
habit, often with the dancing master's help.
Awkwardness creates prejudice; stumbling in manner suggests insecurity
or a lack of confidence. In contrast, openness, freedom,
and self-possession set others at ease, revealing inner harmony. Grace in
women secures affections and signals a well-balanced
soul, just as awkwardness in men impedes gallantry and connection.
 
Lastly, avoid pouring over books until bent double; this habit is hard to
break and harmful to both health and esteem. A stoop
diminishes public and private standing. You are upright now, walking
boldly and spiritedly-preserve this carefully. Elasticity of
limbs and upright deportment is vital to worldly success as much as
actions.
 
Do not, by neglecting how to enter a room properly, stumble at the very
threshold of good graces. Remember, nothing
prejudices people more than awkwardness.

questionText:

Every time a child takes a soft drink, is he laying the ground­work for a
dangerous bone disease? Fizzy and sugary drinks don’t cause
osteoporosis but, because they are often a substitute for a glass of milk,
children miss out on taking in the calcium and vitamin D they need to build
a strong skeleton. Many of them also lead a sedentary lifestyle, so they
aren’t getting the bone­building benefits of vigorous exercise either. These
children tend to suffer from brittle bones and frac­tures later on in life. In
addition, they could be at a risk of being diagnosed with osteoporosis at an
earlier age than most others.
 
Osteoporosis starts in childhood, but its consequences are apparent at a
later stage in life. This condition causes bones to become riddled with
holes, like the framework of a house that has been attacked by termites.
This can lead to broken bones, which in turn, can cause deformity, chronic
pain, and disability. Osteoporosis can be fatal: up to 25 percent of older
people who suffer a broken hip die within a year. Osteoporosis isn’t just
your grandmother’s health threat. Although it strikes over 50 million
women in India, it also menaces over 12 million men.
 
It is important to save millions of people from the risk of suffering from
osteoporosis by adopting preventive measures like walking, jogging or
skipping. Getting enough sunlight, and adequate calcium, especially
through fruits, vegetables and fermented dairy products also helps.
